opening_note: October in San Diego doesn't look like fall. Some of the year's hottest days land this month. But the evenings shorten, the squash is fully cured, the last poblanos are drying into anchos, and the pomegranates are heavy. It's the first month worth turning the oven on for an hour.

field_notes.name: An ancho is a poblano that waited.
field_notes.body: Leave a poblano on the plant until it turns red, dry it in the sun, and it becomes an ancho — wrinkled, nearly black, and smelling faintly of raisins. The chile you charred in September and the one in this month's jar are the same pepper, a few weeks apart. That's the whole season in one ingredient.

field_notes.name: Halfway up, never over.
field_notes.body: The one rule of a braise: after you brown the meat, the liquid comes about halfway up it, not over the top. What's under the surface goes soft and turns to stew; what's above it stays browned, and the skin crisps again in the oven. Drown it and you've made soup. Every braise you make this winter works the same way.

field_notes.name: Seed a pomegranate underwater.
field_notes.body: Score around the crown, pull the fruit apart into sections, and hold them in a bowl of cold water while you push the seeds out with your thumbs. The seeds sink. The pith floats. Skim it, drain, and you have a cup of seeds and no red kitchen.

field_notes.name: October at the fish counter.
field_notes.body: California spiny lobster season opens the first weekend of October, and for the first few weeks it is genuinely local, genuinely live, and worth one splurge. Ask for it split. Broil it with butter and garlic and eat it the way it's eaten an hour south: beans, rice, flour tortillas, lime. If it isn't there, the question from July still works: not 'Do you have salmon?' but 'What came in today?'

weekend_meal.name: Dutch-oven chicken with delicata and white beans.
weekend_meal.intro: One meal should feel like the reason you went shopping. In October, it's the first one that asks for the oven for an hour — and the reason to get the heavy pot back out.
weekend_meal.card_line: Bone-in chicken thighs, delicata, white beans, poblano, rosemary, lemon
ingredients: 6 bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs, about 2½ lbs
1 delicata squash — halved, seeded, cut into 1-inch half-moons, skin on
2 poblanos, seeded and cut into strips
2 cans cannellini beans, drained and rinsed
2 cups chicken stock, or 2 tsp bouillon in 2 cups hot water
Olive oil, kosher salt, black pepper
weekend_meal.ingredient_note: Any heavy, lidded, oven-safe pot will do if you don't have a Dutch oven. Salt the chicken the night before if you remember; right before is fine if you don't.
weekend_meal.method: Heat the oven to 375°F. Pat the chicken dry and salt both sides. In the Dutch oven over medium-high, with a thin film of oil, lay the thighs skin side down and leave them alone for 8 to 10 minutes, until the skin is deep golden and lets go on its own. Turn them for two minutes, then set them aside and pour off all but two tablespoons of fat. Add the poblano, garlic, and rosemary and stir for three or four minutes. Pour in a splash of stock and scrape up everything stuck to the bottom — that's the flavor. Add the beans, squash, and the rest of the stock, season, and nestle the chicken back in skin side up, with the liquid about halfway up the thighs. Into the oven, lid off, for 45 minutes, until the squash is tender and the meat pulls from the bone. Zest the lemon over the pot and squeeze in half of it. Let it sit ten minutes. Salsa macha at the table. It's better the next day, pulled off the bone and eaten over rice.

drink.name: South Park Shrub
drink.intro: One drink. Make the base once and it lasts the week.
season_adds: A thin slice of apple, optional
drink.method: Press the seeds from one pomegranate through a strainer to get about half a cup of juice; save a spoonful of whole seeds. Stir the juice with two tablespoons of cider vinegar and two tablespoons of sugar until the sugar dissolves. That's the shrub — it keeps a week in the fridge. For a glass: two tablespoons over ice, topped with sparkling water, a few seeds on top. It should taste sharp first and sweet second.

local_ritual.label: San Diego ritual
local_ritual.name: Walk out for the lobster opener.
local_ritual.description: Lobster season opens at dusk on the first weekend of October, and the piers on Shelter Island fill with hoop nets and headlamps. You don't need to fish. Walk out after dark with something warm, watch the first nets come up, and notice that you wanted the jacket — the first night of the year that's true.

one_thing_to_notice.headline: The corners on a pomegranate.
one_thing_to_notice.body: An underripe pomegranate is round. As the seeds swell, they press out against the skin until the fruit goes slightly squared-off, with flat faces and soft ridges. The angular ones are the full ones. Once you see it, you'll stop picking the pretty round one.

delicata-squash.name: Delicata squash
delicata-squash.tile_uses: Roasted, pasta, beside salmon, the weekend braise
delicata-squash.why_now: September brought the first ones. By October they've cured longer — more orange down in the grooves, sweeter inside — and they cost less. It's the squash in the weekend braise, and the one worth keeping two of on the counter all month.
how_to_choose: Orange in the grooves between the green stripes means longer cured and sweeter
Firm all over, with no soft or wet spots at either end
Heavy for its size
A dry, intact stem still attached
Small to medium; the large ones get watery
delicata-squash.buy_this_much: 3. Two for roasting through the week, one for the pot on the weekend.
delicata-squash.price_note: Cheaper than it was in September, and still sold by the piece — the medium ones are the better buy.

delicata-squash.weekend_use: Cut into thick half-moons and braised with bone-in chicken thighs, white beans, poblano, and rosemary — the weekend meal.
delicata-squash.storage: On the counter, out of the sun, for a month. It doesn't want the fridge. Once cut, wrap it and use it within four days.
delicata-squash.one_thing_to_learn: Delicata holds its shape in a braise where butternut would collapse. The thin skin you don't peel is structure. For the pot, cut it thick — an inch — so it turns tender when the chicken does, not before.

poblanos.name: The last poblanos
poblanos.tile_uses: The weekend braise, rice bowls, tacos, the freezer
poblanos.why_now: Roasting chiles run from late August to about mid-October, then they're gone until next year. The ones still around this month are often blushing red — a little sweeter, sometimes a little hotter. Left longer, they become anchos, which is where this month's jar starts.
how_to_choose: Glossy and heavy, with no wrinkles
Flat-sided ones char more evenly
A red blush means riper — sweeter, and sometimes hotter
Skip anything soft at the shoulders
poblanos.buy_this_much: 4–6. Two go into the braise raw. Char the rest and freeze the strips for November.
poblanos.price_note: Still cheap for the first two weeks. After that, what's left is whatever didn't sell.

flavor_paths.name: Raw, cooked in fat
flavor_paths.description: Sliced into strips, softened with garlic. Green and grassy. The braise.

flavor_paths.name: Charred
flavor_paths.description: September's move: blacken, steam, peel. Smoky strips for bowls and tacos.

weekday_uses: Charred strips in a rice bowl with sweet potato

poblanos.weekend_use: Sliced raw into the Dutch oven with garlic and rosemary, as the aromatic under the weekend braise.
poblanos.storage: Raw, a week in the crisper. Charred and peeled, four days in the fridge — or freeze the strips flat in a bag and break off what you need.
poblanos.one_thing_to_learn: Raw poblano and charred poblano are two different vegetables. Sliced raw and cooked in fat, it's green and grassy, doing what a bell pepper does with more to say. Charred, it's smoky and soft. The braise wants the first; the rice bowl wants the second.

sweet-potatoes.name: Sweet potatoes
sweet-potatoes.tile_uses: Rice bowls, tacos, beside anything roasted
sweet-potatoes.why_now: Most of California's sweet potatoes come out of the ground around Merced in September and October. The new crop is on the shelves now — at its cheapest, and not yet tired from months in storage.
how_to_choose: Firm all over, with no soft ends
No sprouts and no wrinkling
Medium and even in shape, so they cook at one speed
Orange-fleshed (garnet or jewel) for roasting
sweet-potatoes.buy_this_much: 2 lbs. They keep, so they're the thing you cook the week it gets away from you.
sweet-potatoes.price_note: Cheapest of the year through November, when the holidays push the price back up.

sweet-potatoes.storage: Somewhere cool and dark, not the fridge — cold turns the center hard and odd-tasting. They keep for weeks.
sweet-potatoes.one_thing_to_learn: Cut side down is the whole trick. The flat face sits on the hot pan, the sugars caramelize into a dark crust, and the inside steams in its own skin. Flip it halfway and you lose the crust. Leave it alone for thirty-five minutes.

apples.name: Late Julian apples
apples.why_now: September's apples were for eating raw. October's are Julian's late ones — Granny Smith, Pink Lady, Winesap — tarter and firmer, which is exactly what you want in a hot pan. They hold their shape next to pork instead of turning to sauce.
how_to_choose: Firm, with no give near the stem
Tart varieties for the pan; sweeter ones for eating
The blossom end should smell like apple
Taut skin, not waxy
Ask which ones hold up to heat
apples.buy_this_much: 4–6. Two for the pan, the rest for eating. Buy them weekly; crisp is the point.
apples.price_note: Julian's orchards thin out by the end of the month. Buy them early if you're driving up.

apples.storage: In the fridge, away from anything that absorbs smells. Cold, they stay crisp for weeks.
apples.one_thing_to_learn: A cooking apple is just a tart, firm one. Sugar makes an apple collapse under heat; acid and density hold it together. That's why September said don't bake them yet, and October says go ahead.

pomegranates.why_now: Southern California grows pomegranates, and they ripen in October and November. A heavy one bought now keeps for weeks and turns anything rich into something brighter.

pomegranates.one_thing_to_learn: Pomegranate is October's lime: something sharp to put against heavier food. Rich things need acid — lemon in the braise, cider vinegar in the shrub, pomegranate on the squash. Same move, different ingredient.

fuyu-persimmons.name: Fuyu persimmons
fuyu-persimmons.tile_uses: Sliced raw, with cheese, on yogurt
fuyu-persimmons.why_now: Fuyus come from North County groves, usually in the last weeks of the month — so don't go looking on the first. When they turn up, they're one of the best things in the store, and almost nobody knows what to do with them.
how_to_choose: Squat and flat on top, shaped like a tomato — that's a Fuyu

fuyu-persimmons.storage: On the counter until they give very slightly, then the fridge for a week or two.
fuyu-persimmons.one_thing_to_learn: The two persimmons in the bin are not interchangeable. A firm Hachiya is so tannic it dries out your whole mouth; it has to go completely soft first. A Fuyu has no such problem and is good crisp. Learn the shape and you'll never make the mistake.
